title: Lottery Prior: Randomized Neural Compression for Zero-Shot Inverse Problems
claim: A lightweight two-phase method of zero-shot learning then randomized-network restoration outperforms existing solvers across diverse inverse tasks.
layout: 2 stacked sections, top pipeline flows left-to-right, bottom radar chart
description: The figure has two parts split by a dashed line. The top is a two-phase pipeline in rounded gray boxes. In the Zero-shot Learning Phase, a degraded parrot image goes through a loop with a pruned network (binary mask, scissors, flame icons for trainable parts). A modulation vector shown as a red triangular grid of blue-green cells is added to it. An entropy model (green box) regularizes the modulation vector. Red arrows lead down to the Restoration Phase. There, random seeds feed an initialization step that produces frozen (snowflake) randomized networks. These are masked and modulated, with ⊗ symbols and red modulation bars, to form the Lottery Priors, which output a clean parrot reconstruction. The bottom is a hexagonal radar chart that compares four methods on six tasks: denoising, super-resolution and inpainting. The red Lottery Prior polygon encloses the others, with its scores in bold red. A legend sits below the chart.
caption: Up: Illustration of Lottery Priors for zero-shot inverse
abstract: We study zero-shot inverse problems, where a clean signal is recovered from a single degraded observation without external training data. Contrary to the common belief that such problems require highly complex models, we show that a lightweight neural network, when combined with entropy and complexity regularization in a compression-based formulation, is sufficient for high-quality restoration. We propose Lottery Prior, a compression-based inverse solver that leverages architectural priors from random networks and induces a family of implicit priors through randomness, enabling ensemble-based refinement. We further derive non-asymptotic error bounds for compression-based maximum-likelihood inverse solvers, revealing how rate–distortion constraints act as implicit regularizers. Experiments on denoising, noisy super-resolution, and inpainting demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art with significantly fewer effective parameters.
